turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Thanks for fitting us in, I know it's a mad morning. It's the appendix wound, ten days since they took it out, the open one not the keyhole, and the skin round it has gone red and I've been worrying at it since I woke up.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ten days exactly?

[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten days, yes. Tuesday before last, in theatre late morning, home on the Thursday, and my sister put a circle on the calendar so today is day ten, not day nine. I double-checked because I always muck the counting up.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weeping, or just red?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Both, really. A yellowy smear on the pad, not pouring. When it started I cannot tell you, Friday or Saturday, I keep flipping, the days have blurred with the school run.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I saw it yesterday arvo. Moist, yellow, more than the day before.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Last night I was boiling, proper teeth-chattering, then I took Panadol and by this morning the temperature felt normal. I'm not hot sitting here.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Number on the thermometer?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Thirty-eight point two, I think. I was half asleep and the digits are tiny on that thing.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I read it. Thirty-eight point four. She shook for a good hour.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not once. Appetite's a bit off, toast mostly, but I haven't been sick, not even in the car, which is usually when I feel crook.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Diarrhoea?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Once a day, same as before the operation. Sorry, that's more than you asked.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pain at the wound?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, a burning sore right on the scar. Worse if I cough or if my jeans rub. It had been easing, then two days ago it cranked back up, which is what spooked me.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tracking up the abdomen?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Just the bottom end of the scar. It isn't creeping anywhere, I checked in the mirror twice.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breathless? Chest pain?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No and no. Lungs feel fine. I walked from the car park without puffing, which actually surprised me.
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Community nurse was in this morning. She took the dressing off, said it looked angry with a bit of ooze, stuck a fresh pad on. No swab.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dressing's off. About four centimetres of redness around the lower end, a little yellow discharge, the edges are holding, and there's nothing fluctuant under it.

[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): That's the stinging spot. I think it smells faintly sweet, though he reckons I'm imagining that. The tape also took a bit of skin off the side, which has been its own little drama.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Could be a stitch coming out, could be an early wound infection. I am not calling either until a swab. No diagnosis today.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Still taking the hospital antibiotic?

[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Finished them. Keflex, those capsules. Five days... or was it seven? The chemist label was smudged. Last dose was Tuesday, unless it was Wednesday night in front of the telly.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The discharge sheet says cephalexin, seven days. She's been saying five all week.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Dose?

[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Five hundred milligrams, I think. Could've been the two-fifty. Big white capsules, three times a day. I missed a couple on the weekend, sports carnival, the kids, you know how that goes.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Other medicines?

[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Panadol when it hurts, and Nurofen if that's not enough. The little pink biotin tablets in my bag are my sister's, for her hair, I haven't touched them. My husband takes metformin for his sugar, that's his, not mine, he just drove.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Panadol dose?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Five hundred milligram tablets, two at a time, so a gram. About three times yesterday, not on a clock, just when the burning got loud.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nurofen?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Two hundred milligram tablets. One, sometimes two. Twice yesterday, after food, because otherwise my stomach complains.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Penicillin allergy? Any drug allergy?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None. Penicillin loads of times, no rash, no swelling, nothing ever.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Correct. No allergies.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Course is done, so we watch it. Repeat the Keflex only if it hasn't settled. See you next week.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was shaking with that fever, and the ooze is worse than yesterday. Watching it doesn't sit right with me.

[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): And I'm washed out today, properly flat, even with a normal temp. Parking was a circus and there's assembly at school, but the red bit looks angrier than when the nurse saw it, I swear.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then watching is the wrong plan. I'll swab it now and change the antibiotic to flucloxacillin. No more Keflex.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Flucloxacillin, right, the skin-bug one? Will it turn my stomach? After the op I lived on toast and dry biscuits, Vegemite, no butter, I can give you the whole menu.
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Five hundred milligrams, four times a day, by mouth, seven days. Empty stomach if you can manage. For the wound.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Swab goes today. If it grows something odd we can revisit, but you start the fluclox now regardless.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): Dressings? Showers? Mum said air it, the nurse said cover it, I've been doing a sad halfway house and patting it with a clean towel, which may be nonsense.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep a clean dry dressing on. Change it if it soaks through. Shower, no bath.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you in two days, swab or not, better or not.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads or the fever comes back before then, come straight in.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): What if the fluclox makes me queasy the way the Keflex did on day two? Not vomiting, just green, biscuits fixed it, and it passed. I don't want to muck the course up.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you can't keep the tablets down, ring us. Don't stop them on your own. Otherwise finish the seven days.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll grab the script at the chemist. She'll forget the midday one unless I nag, same as the Keflex.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Script is fluclox only. Do not restart the Keflex. Reception will book the two days.

[SEG0055] person_1 (PATIENT): My gallbladder scar from years back never did any of this, that one was tiny and boring, so this has thrown me. There's a yellow line on the car so we should bolt. Swab, fluclox, dressing on, back in two days. Thanks.
[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Off you go.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Keflex/cephalexin, post-op, discontinued, TID, 5-7 days supported; dose uncertain between 500 mg and 250 mg.
bad.text: Keflex (generic_name=cephalexin, dose=500 mg, frequency=three times a day, duration=approximately 5 to 7 days, indication=hospital antibiotic after the operation, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Fever included rigors/teeth-chattering shaking for about an hour last night.
Bowels were normal: once a day, same as before the operation.
No penicillin allergy specifically, with prior penicillin exposure and no rash or swelling.

Recent cephalexin timing/adherence details are incomplete/wrongly captured: family member said the discharge sheet specified cephalexin for 7 days; patient said last dose was Tuesday or Wednesday night and missed a couple of weekend doses.
Ibuprofen was taken after food because otherwise it upsets her stomach.
Doctor expressed diagnostic uncertainty: could be a stitch coming out or an early wound infection, and would not call either before a swab; no diagnosis today.
Community nurse reviewed the wound the same morning, found it looked 'angry' with a bit of ooze, replaced the dressing, and did not take a swab.
Additional local symptoms/findings mentioned but not recorded: patient reported faintly sweet smell from the wound and tape-related skin stripping beside the wound.
Follow-up wording was stronger than recorded: doctor would see her in two days 'swab or not, better or not'.

omissions.text: Measured fever value was disputed: patient said 38.2 C but family member said she read 38.4 C and that the patient shook for a good hour.
The family member expressed disagreement with the initial plan to just watch it, saying the shaking fever and worsening ooze made that plan not sit right with her.

Initial plan was changed: the doctor first said to watch it, repeat Keflex only if it had not settled, and see her next week, but then reversed this and changed to swab plus flucloxacillin with review in two days.
